extracted.intended_audience: improvisers, improv students and workshop participants
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for performing improvisation in public and for workshop practice: scene-building, emotional stakes, rule-use, and first-show preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greatest Hits Tape / let go of bad moments
rubrics_metrics.description: Close your eyes, replay a terrible moment, let it go; then play back your best moments repeatedly to reinforce your talent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make a mental 'Greatest Hits Tape' of your best workshop/show moments and play it often to build confidence; do the reverse with bad moments—see them, breathe out, and discard them. Use before auditions or shows. This reinforces memory of success and combats tendency to obsess over failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question rules rather than obey slavishly
rubrics_metrics.description: There are principles that help improvisers learn, but slavish obedience to rules (taught as training wheels) can stagnate improvisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regularly ask 'Why is that rule there and what would happen if we broke it?' Use rules as exercises or training wheels; be prepared to break them thoughtfully when experienced and when it serves the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: NEVER ASK A QUESTION (reconsidered)
rubrics_metrics.description: The common injunction 'never ask a question' is challenged: questions can drive drama and make characters vulnerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't reflexively ban questions; a question like 'How would you feel if I told you I'd never loved you?' can be the motor of a scene. Beware the anti-pattern of statements that add nothing. Use questions to create uncertainty, vulnerability, and dramatic stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: KNOW THE OTHER PERSON (rule critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule 'always know the person you are talking to for at least six months' is unrealistic and eliminates many dramatic/romantic/first-meeting scenarios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't restrict yourself to pre-existing relationships; first-meeting dynamics are valuable (romcoms, detective, hospital scenarios). Use whatever relationship serves the scene rather than rigidly following this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never Argue, Always Agree (re-evaluation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The injunction to always agree (yes-and) can eliminate conflict; effective scenes require disagreement and strong reactions at points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use agreement to build a platform but allow/introduce conflict when it raises stakes. If performers always agree, scenes can stagnate. Aim for big reactions and emotional argument where appropriate; call partners out if they trivialize everything.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid transaction scenes (rethink)
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers who ban shop/transaction scenes are limiting possibilities; transaction settings can produce strong change if the characters are affected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't rule out locations like shops or classrooms—Monty Python's Cheese Shop and many sitcom/classroom scenes prove these can work when they create change, vulnerability, or affect characters deeply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid teaching scenes (rethink)
rubrics_metrics.description: Banning teaching scenes to avoid repetition is shortsighted; teaching scenes can work when they produce genuine change and deeper emotional stakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use teaching-as-transformation (e.g., Dirty Dancing) where lessons change characters emotionally. Focus on how the teacher/learner are affected, not on rote instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use rules as exercises/training wheels
rubrics_metrics.description: Many rules are intended to correct bad habits for beginners; they should strengthen skills rather than limit long-term action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat rules as temporary exercises. As you gain experience, evaluate and selectively break rules. If a rule doesn't make sense to you or to the comedy you love, analyze and adapt it.

rubrics_metrics.name: START IN THE MIDDLE (but be flexible)
rubrics_metrics.description: The common teaching to 'start in the middle' avoids dull beginnings, but starting at the beginning can be valid and liberating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open to starting scenes at the beginning when it helps establish a satisfying emotional arc. Don't feel cultish about techniques—explore different approaches and learn from other teachers/companies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for big reactions to everyday situations
rubrics_metrics.description: Most great comedy comes from performers having large, often childish or extreme reactions to small, everyday provocations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than trivializing everything, allow characters to be truly affected by small incidents (e.g., TiVo erased)—audiences recognize and enjoy exaggerated, emotionally honest responses (Frasier, Seinfeld, Cartman). This creates recognition and catharsis rather than mere 'tickling'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid trivializing serious situations (use affects appropriately)
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvisers often trivialize grave situations (bathos), which can produce only mild laughs; better to let characters be genuinely affected when stakes require it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use serious feeling when warranted and keep scenes consistent—if the premise promises emotional change, deliver it. Conversely, if you intend comedy from triviality, use exaggerated emotion in a way the audience recognizes as cathartic/funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be vulnerable and show change
rubrics_metrics.description: Audiences come to see people changed and emotionally affected; vulnerability and transformation are central to satisfying scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose vulnerability deliberately (ask for stakes that could make you embarrassed or hurt) and allow scenes to produce lasting change in character or relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish environment and relationship (build a platform)
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin by physically building an environment: look around, open a door, pick up objects to show where you are and what you want.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use physical action to create a playground for exploration. Encourage partners to enter after the environment is set so you have elements to play off. Example: open a cupboard, take something out, establish if you're roommates or lab partners, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start positive/stable, then allow change
rubrics_metrics.description: If you tend to start with conflict, try agreeing/building a platform and being positive until a partner introduces something that affects you negatively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use agreement initially to build the scene's world; then let conflict or thwarting of desires create the emotional turn. This helps avoid scenes that stagnate in early bickering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thwart desire to create stakes and affect characters
rubrics_metrics.description: The easiest way to affect a character is to thwart their desire—deny or complicate what the character wants to raise stakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once you know what the character wants (relaxing night, stealing lab rats, meet a scientist), introduce obstacles that force emotional reactions and change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reincorporation to close a scene
rubrics_metrics.description: Reincorporate an element from the beginning (an object, line, or action) at the end to signal the scene is over and to make the scene feel clever and complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look back and reuse items (Coke can, remote control, skeleton key) in the climax or resolution. This gives the audience the pleasure of recognition and signals payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow variety in show structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles are shapes, not formulas; a show should have variety—don't force every scene into the same pattern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the principles (start stable, be changed, reincorporate) when helpful, but abandon them if something better is happening; different scenes (e.g., grave-digging opening in the middle) can still deliver promise and payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get onstage early—don't wait to be 'ready'
rubrics_metrics.description: The only way to become ready is to perform; get your first gig within months, and early shows accelerate learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange a first show with your teachers or group; three months is enough to prepare students. Use short slots (10–15 minutes) if needed and share stage time with experienced groups to build experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invite friends and family to fill the house
rubrics_metrics.description: Bring lots of people to your first shows so the audience feels full and individual performers feel anonymous and less exposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A full house reduces fear and creates a friendlier atmosphere. Ask fellow students to invite guests as well to create a supportive audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage pre-show time: arrive early and warm up
rubrics_metrics.description: Get there promptly to acclimatize, warm up with fellow players, and avoid last-minute panic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrive with spare time for travel delays, know where the theatre is, and warm up physically and vocally with the group. Falling in ten minutes before performance is a bad practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't over-plan or obsess about the show during the day
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid spending the whole day fretting or rehearsing plans that will hinder spontaneity on stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do distracting activities during the day to take your mind off the show. Walk onstage ready to see what shows up rather than following a rigid plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: I Suck And I Love To Fail (attitude toward mistakes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt an attitude of embracing failure; if you screw up but stay happy, the audience will love you and you'll enjoy the experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use exercises that normalize failure and maintain positivity. This reduces fear of loss of status and encourages risk-taking onstage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle director interference pragmatically
rubrics_metrics.description: If a director is padding their part or interfering unnecessarily, complaining on stage won't help; consider replacing or omitting them and test whether the audience enjoys the show more without them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you and the director genuinely have simultaneous ideas (in sync), it's fine. If the director obstructs, remove them to see if the show improves—the only way to find out if something works is to try it.
